QuantiBias: Benchmarking Quantization-Induced Bias in LLMs

Emilio Ferrara Affiliation: Thomas Lord Department of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Southern California Email: emiliofe@usc.edu
Abstract

Almost every large language model that reaches a broad audience is quantized: trained in full precision, then compressed for efficiency. This step is assumed harmless and its safety is rarely re-checked. We find its principal side effect is increased bias that standard safety evaluation misses. Holding the model, its training, and the prompts fixed, a quantized model still refuses harmful requests, still avoids over-refusing benign prompts, and still selects the unbiased multiple-choice answer. Yet asked an open-ended question, the same model volunteers stereotypes in all eight languages we probe, in roughly one in four open-ended answers under an independent judge (~24% to ~27% across the compression ladder): it passes every standard check and still reaches users measurably more biased. The selective gap is a robust finding; whether open-ended bias further increases with compression is less certain, sensitive to the judge that scores it. We address both with QuantiBias, a benchmark that pairs a generative, multilingual stereotype probe with the refusal and multiple-choice controls that isolate open-ended generation, contrasts each build with and without reasoning, and rates the content severity of what it generates. Across two backbone models (Qwen and Gemma), a five-family screen, and eight benchmarks, quantizers allocate their extra precision by capability data that carries no bias-prevention signal, and reasoning before answering roughly halves the effect on some families while doing nothing on others. A quantized build must be re-evaluated for open-ended bias, not only on the short-form safeguards it already passes. Code and baselines: https://huggingface.co/datasets/emilioferrara/quantibias.

1 Introduction

A language model is evaluated at full precision and typically deployed compressed. Post-training quantization shrinks the weights before release, often by a factor of 3 to 14, so the build a user interacts with is usually not the one the evaluation measured. Quantization is expected to preserve behavior, and capability benchmarks largely bear this out; the safety and bias side has been probed less systematically. Reports on aggressively quantized builds tend to document capability retention across benchmarks while saying less about safety or bias.

Two prior results suggest this gap is consequential. The butterfly-effect account of AI bias (Ferrara, 2024) shows that small perturbations to a model or its training pipeline can produce disproportionate and hard-to-predict changes in bias. Quantization is an unusually clean perturbation of this kind: it alters no training data, no objective, and no prompt, only the numerical precision of the weights. Separately, a multi-dimensional audit of targeted bias-reduction methods (Chand et al., 2026) found that reducing bias on one dimension often shifted it on dimensions the method did not target, with smaller models affected more, which the authors attribute to entangled representations in which no adjustment stays local. Together these results predict that quantization moves behavior on several axes at once: it perturbs every weight simultaneously, is directed at no particular behavior, and, if representations are entangled, does not confine its effects to the capabilities it preserves.

Prior studies of quantization and safety often disagree, and much of the disagreement follows from what the standard safety metric examines. Safety is usually summarized as the rate at which a short harmful prompt succeeds. That measure averages over the brief exchanges in which quantization does the least damage, and never examines the sustained, open-ended generation in which it does the most; separating the two shows the short-form safeguards holding while open-ended generation carries bias the checks never sample. Two measurement details compound the confusion, and we control both: a build’s nominal label understates how much it is quantized, so grouping builds by label compares models compressed to different degrees as though they were the same; and the precision at which a model runs its matrix multiplications depends on the serving kernel as well as the stored weights, so two byte-identical checkpoints can compute at different precision. We therefore index every result to effective bits per weight measured from the artifact (Section 3).

This paper makes three contributions. First, we document selective blindness: across two anchor backbones, a five-family screen, and eight benchmarks, quantization leaves the safeguards standard evaluations measure, refusal and multiple-choice bias avoidance, unchanged, while the bias a model volunteers in open-ended generation goes unmeasured by them. Second, we give the mechanism (Section 7): quantizers allocate precision to calibration data that carries no bias signal, leaving the bias-relevant weights fragile, and we show when reasoning before answering suppresses the effect and when it does not: reasoning halves the open-ended bias on Qwen but leaves it unchanged on Gemma. Third, we build the instrument that detects the gap. We introduce QuantiBias, a benchmark that pairs a generative, multilingual stereotype probe with the refusal and multiple-choice controls that establish the effect is specific to open-ended generation, contrasts each build with and without reasoning, and rates the content severity of what a model generates (Section 4).

2 Related Work

Quantization is known to change model behavior beyond the capability benchmarks used to validate it, and its effect on safety and bias has been studied unevenly. Xu et al. (2024) evaluate pruning and quantization along degeneration harm, representational harm, and dialect bias, and show that generation-side safety can erode while task accuracy holds. Closest to our setting, Marcuzzi et al. (2026) extend this across 13 benchmarks and report that aggressive quantization slightly raises stereotyping and bias in generative tasks while lowering toxicity and leaving sentiment flat. Rath and Maliakkal (2026) find that three-bit quantization turns 6 to 21% of previously unbiased BBQ items stereotypical, and Hua et al. (2026) show that such flips often cancel in aggregate, masking large per-group swings. On the safety side, Kharinaev et al. (2025) document alignment degradation across 66 quantized variants, Egashira et al. (2024) show that quantization can be weaponized adversarially so the artifact a user evaluates is not the one they deploy, and Al Hakim et al. (2026) protect bias-critical weights and find the damage worst in non-English settings.

We build on these findings and depart from them in three ways. First, we isolate a selectivity effect that aggregate reporting obscures: the short-form safeguards these evaluations rely on, refusal and multiple-choice bias avoidance, stay flat while the bias a model volunteers in open-ended generation rises (Jin et al., 2025), so a build passes the checks and reaches users more biased. Second, we test whether reasoning acts as a safeguard and find that it does not hold universally: on the Gemma backbone, unlike Qwen, reasoning does not reduce the bias. Third, we add a content-severity axis that rates the harmfulness of what a model actually generates, which no prior compression study measures. Throughout, we index results to effective bits per weight measured from the artifact rather than nominal quantizer labels, which vary in what they deliver (Section 3). Where critical-weight protection changes how a model is quantized, QuantiBias changes how it is evaluated.

3 Measuring True Quantization

A build’s name states a nominal bits-per-weight, but conventional low-bit builds retain some components, the embeddings, attention, and output head, at substantially higher precision, and the size of that hidden margin varies from build to build and vendor to vendor. We therefore measure every model directly, reading the size and quantization type of each stored weight tensor and dividing total weight bytes by parameter count to obtain the effective bits per weight (bpw). Table 1 gives the two anchor ladders; nominal labels overstate the degree of quantization by 11 to 40% (Figure A3).

Two consequences follow. First, from here on we plot every result against measured bits per weight, and the label serves only to identify the artifact. Second, weight precision does not fully specify the treatment: the checkpoint does not determine whether the model’s matrix multiplications run in 16-bit or 4-bit, so we record the resolved backend for every run and treat the weight measurement as a partial description. The label understates quantization because the high-precision components are hidden behind it. In the “2-bit” UD-IQ2_XXS build the multilayer-perceptron weights sit at 2.14 bits while the output head and attention tensors carry substantially more (4.53 and 3.55 bits), and the build mixes nine distinct quantization types; normalization tensors stay at full 32-bit precision. This mixing is inherent to the llama.cpp k-quant schemes these builds use (Gerganov and others, 2023), which, like activation-aware and error-compensating post-training quantizers (Frantar et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2023), allocate more bits to weights they judge sensitive; that allocation is tuned on capability data and has no reason to track bias. The end-to-end ternary and one-bit builds, following the trend toward natively low-bit models (Ma et al., 2024), are the exception, holding perceptron, attention, and output head at a single flat precision, which is why their measured value tracks their label far more closely.

4 QuantiBias

QuantiBias packages the open-ended bias measurement into a reusable protocol with four components.

  1. 1.

    A generative, paired, multilingual probe. Each item is an open-ended request that gives a model room to volunteer or decline a stereotype, paired with a stereotype-endorsing claim and its group-swapped counterpart that fix the axis a judge scores (Section 6). Open generation surfaces bias that multiple-choice instruments miss (Jin et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024). A parallel-translated variant holds content fixed while varying only the language. Multilingual bias suites exist, but each drops one of these axes: MBBQ is multiple-choice (Neplenbroek et al., 2024), the Multilingual Holistic Bias set scores template sentences rather than free generation (Costa-jussà et al., 2023), and SHADES supplies parallel stereotypes without a compression axis (Mitchell et al., 2025). Our probe is, to our knowledge, the only one that is open-ended, parallel across eight languages, and rated for the harmfulness of what a model volunteers.

  2. 2.

    Scoring against measured effective bpw. QuantiBias reports every result against the measured precision of a build (Section 3), never its nominal label, so two builds sharing a label but differing in real precision are not conflated.

  3. 3.

    A reasoning-load contrast. Each build is evaluated with deliberation enabled and disabled, because the effect is concentrated on the non-deliberative path and its remediability is family-dependent; a single mode hides both.

  4. 4.

    Controls that show the effect is selective. QuantiBias pairs the generative probe with refusal, over-refusal, and multiple-choice bias measures. Their flatness separates selective bias amplification from a general behavioral change.

A build passes QuantiBias when its generative-bias rate does not rise across its own precision ladder while the controls stay flat, and fails when generative bias rises even though the controls do not, the signature this paper documents. We release the probe, measurement code, and scoring harness.11 1 Code, rubrics, and baseline results: https://huggingface.co/datasets/emilioferrara/quantibias

5 Experiments

Instrumentation.

Each evaluation cell is one (artifact, benchmark, arm, prompt-pool, decoding) tuple, executed by a checkpointed, idempotent harness that writes verbatim generations to an append-only store; every reported number traces to a job identifier and a content hash. Decoding is held constant across precisions (temperature 0.7, top-pp 0.95, fixed token budgets, the model’s own chat template). We score the full-ladder generative probe with an in-family Qwen3-8B lean judge, which is fast enough to run at scale, and validate that scoring with two independent judges drawn from different vendors and from families outside the evaluation set: Claude Sonnet-5 (Anthropic) and Gemini-2.5-pro (Google), both fixed frontier models never themselves quantized, so the quantization under test cannot affect the instrument that measures them. The lean judge’s validated quantity is the binary neutral-versus-endorsing distinction, which it recovers at about 94% against MBTP’s own labeled reference responses; its absolute endorsement level is judge-family-dependent and far below what the independent judges assign.22 2 “In-family” means the judge, Qwen3-8B, is from the same model family as the anchor under test, so it cannot independently measure the bias level (Wataoka et al., 2024); the two out-of-family judges (Claude Sonnet-5 and Gemini-2.5-pro) supply that. On the open generations the in-family judge scores well below them, so its rates understate the level, and the selective gap rests on the independent judges. What we claim is the selective gap: the short-form safeguards stay flat while open-ended generation carries a high stereotype rate under every judge we ran. The compression slope of that open-ended rate is a within-judge comparison and is not established: re-scoring the reasoning-off ladder with an independent judge returns a high but roughly flat profile (0.238, 0.267, 0.266 from Q4 to one bit), against the rising 0.042, 0.053, 0.078 the lean judge reports, so we treat the dose-response as provisional (Limitations). On a controlled parallel probe (two middle rungs, n=160n=160) the two independent judges agree on 85% of items (Krippendorff’s α=0.69\alpha=0.69), and a full-ladder independent-ensemble re-scoring is the reference measurement, whose levels supersede the lean judge’s.

Benchmarks.

The first group tests explicit safeguards: refusal of directly harmful requests and their jailbreak-wrapped versions (StrongREJECT (Souly et al., 2024)), over-refusal of benign-but-alarming prompts (XSTest (Röttger et al., 2024)), and multiple-choice bias avoidance under ambiguity (BBQ (Parrish et al., 2022)). The second measures implicit behavior with a multilingual generative stereotype probe, MBTP (Kaneko et al., 2026), spanning 8 languages (Arabic, Chinese, English, French, German, Japanese, Russian, Spanish) and 13 social categories (Table A1). Each of its items pairs an open-ended request with a matched pair of short claims, one stereotype-endorsing and one its group-swapped counterpart, that fix the axis the judge scores. The probe items are due to (Kaneko et al., 2026); QuantiBias contributes the frozen 320-item balanced subset, the measurement of results against effective bpw, the reasoning-load contrast, and the independent-judge scoring harness. An independent generative benchmark (CEB (Wang et al., 2024)) provides a second instrument over disjoint items; a next-token benchmark (StereoSet (Nadeem et al., 2021)) serves as a short-form negative control; and 2 capability anchors (MMLU-Redux (Gema et al., 2025), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021)) separate safety-specific degradation from general capability loss.

Multilingual construction.

MBTP is built parallel across the eight languages by machine translation with back-translation quality control. Forty English source items are canonical; each is rendered into the other seven languages by a frontier model (Gemini 2.5 Pro), holding the content fixed so that only the language of presentation varies. Every translated field is independently back-translated (Gemini 2.5 Flash) and scored against its source for gross drift, with low-agreement rows flagged rather than dropped and reserved for native-speaker validation. This yields the 320-item parallel probe that isolates the language of presentation from the national target and the content, the confound the original diagonal design carries (cf. Limitations).

6 Results

We establish the effect and its structure on the Qwen3.6-27B anchor, on a second backbone, and across a five-family screen (build details in Table A2). Every rate carries a Wilson 95% interval.

The safety checks hold flat.

Table A3 reports the safeguard, capability, and MBTP benchmarks across the full Qwen3.6-27B ladder, from 16 to 1.13 measured bpw. The safeguards standard evaluations probe do not move: refusal of directly harmful requests stays at 0.98, over-refusal on XSTest near 0.33, and BBQ accuracy under ambiguity near 0.97, at every quantized rung. The capability anchors hold through IQ2 and lose only a little at the one-bit extreme (MMLU-Redux 0.952 to 0.877), which separates safety-specific degradation from general capability loss: from Q4 to IQ2 capability is flat while generative bias already rises. A short-form next-token bias control (StereoSet stereotype score, 50 ideal) is flat as well, 58 to 60 across the ladder. A study measuring only these outcomes would conclude that quantization is safety-neutral. The stable multiple-choice scores may also be flattered by contamination: if BBQ-style items sit in the training data, a model can recognize the evaluation format and answer it well while its open-ended behavior diverges (Balloccu et al., 2024), a defeat device in the sense of Ferrara (2026).

Open-ended bias is high where the safety checks stay flat.

The safeguards hold; open-ended generation does not. On the Qwen3.6-27B anchor the model volunteers a stereotype in a substantial fraction of open-ended answers while its refusal, over-refusal, and multiple-choice bias controls sit at their near-ideal values (Table A3, Figure 2). Under an independent judge that fraction is 0.238, 0.267, and 0.266 across the reasoning-off ladder (per language in Figure A1), close to one open-ended answer in four, while the same model’s multiple-choice bias control stays near 0.97 and its refusal near 0.98 (Limitations), so a build passes every standard check and still reaches users markedly more biased. This selective gap is the robust finding: it is present at every precision and under every judge we ran. Whether the open-ended rate also rises with compression is a second, separable question, and the answer is not universal. Under the in-family lean judge the rate rises at every step on this anchor and every language ends higher at one bit than at 4-bit (Table A3, Figure A5); under the independent judge the same cells are higher and roughly flat. Across the five-family screen the per-family compression slope is not resolved at that sample size: under both judges every Q8-to-Q2 change lies within its 95% interval (Figure 6). We therefore document a selective gap that is robust across judges and families, and a compression-driven increase that appears on the anchor under the lean judge but flattens under the independent one, which we report as provisional. The eight most severe one-bit instances appear in Table 2, one endorsing sentence each; the high-precision build declines each stereotype while the one-bit build asserts it. Appendix D gives the full cards.

Content severity of the endorsements.

Whether a model endorses a stereotype and how harmful the endorsement is are separate questions, and a binary lean answers only the first. We score every one-bit instance the lean judge marked as an endorsement on a 0–4 content-severity rubric (0, no biased content; 4, a biased generalization asserted as fact) with a judge independent of the evaluation set. Of the 48 instances, mean severity is 1.83 and the harm is real but bounded: 33 score 2 or higher (a stated group generalization) while none reach the severity-4 ceiling, so the failure mode is a confident stereotype rather than the most extreme assertion. The rubric also exposes the limits of the binary lean: about a fifth of the instances (10 of 48) score 0, complying with a loaded prompt without asserting the stereotype, a distinction the binary lean cannot make. Table 2 shows the eight most severe instances verbatim and Figure 3 the full distribution; severity is measured at the one-bit rung here, and its slope against compression is a prediction of Section 7 that a higher-powered study could test.

The reasoning contrast, and its limit.

Turning reasoning on roughly halves the rate at every rung and flattens the compression slope from +3.6+3.6 to +0.7+0.7 points (Table A3, Figure A4): compression damages the fast, no-deliberation path. This remedy is not universal (Wu et al., 2025). On the Gemma-4-31B backbone the compression effect replicates (MBTP reasoning off, 0.038 at Q4 rising to 0.069 at IQ2, n=480n{=}480), but reasoning barely moves it: the two modes are identical at Q4 (18 of 480 either way) and close at IQ2 (0.069 off, 0.064 on), against a halving on Qwen (Figure 4). The manipulation did occur, verified by the multi-thousand-character reasoning traces the reasoning-on cells carry. Deliberation is thus a family-dependent safeguard, not a universal one: it helps only where the added reasoning actually revisits the stereotype decision, a mechanism we develop in Section 7.

An independent benchmark agrees.

CEB, a generative bias benchmark sharing no items with MBTP, rises with compression across the Qwen ladder under both judges (n≈960n\approx 960 per rung, reasoning off): the lean judge reports 3.5%3.5\%, 21.9%21.9\%, 24.9%24.9\% and the independent judge 13.5%13.5\%, 23.0%23.0\%, 37.6%37.6\% from Q4 to one bit (Figure 5), the same direction and judge-dependence as MBTP. The one-bit rung is a separate end-to-end ternary backbone, so the robust comparison is the Q4-to-IQ2 rise on the shared Qwen ladder, which both judges show. The effect is therefore not an artifact of the MBTP construction.

Widening to five families.

Screening five model families (Figure 6) resolves the level of open-ended bias but not its per-family compression slope. We hold Qwen3-8B out of the screen because it is the lean judge, which would make the judge and the subject the same model; measured by the independent judge, which has no such conflict, it sits within the retained families’ level band with a slope within noise, so it is excluded for cleanliness, not because it stands out. Baselines differ about twofold across families, with the 8B class above the 27B anchor, consistent with the size fragility reported by Chand et al. (2026). The level is also strongly judge-dependent: an independent re-scoring (Claude Sonnet-5) puts every family at 20 to 30%, three to four times the in-family lean judge, echoing the anchor gap. The per-family slope, by contrast, is within noise at this sample size, under both judges (every Q8-to-Q2 change lies inside its interval), so the screen names which families differ in level without settling whether any one family’s bias rises with compression, which a higher-powered study would resolve.

7 Why the Effect Is Selective

The pattern documented above, refusal intact while open-ended bias worsens as precision falls, is not specific to these models. It follows from how quantization perturbs a network and how generation reads out its state. The account is mechanistic, not a proof; it is consistent with the measurements above.

A bounded, semantically empty perturbation.

Let fWf_{W} denote the model with weights WW and QbQ_{b} quantization to bb bits, so the deployed model is fW+Δbf_{W+\Delta_{b}} with Δb=Qb​(W)−W\Delta_{b}=Q_{b}(W)-W. For round-to-nearest quantization with group scale s∝2−bs\propto 2^{-b}, each weight moves by at most s/2s/2, so 𝔼​‖Δb‖2∝2−2​b\mathbb{E}\,\|\Delta_{b}\|^{2}\propto 2^{-2b}: the perturbation magnitude is set by the measured bit width. This is why we plot against measured bpw.

Discretization at readout.

Each token is selected by an argmax or top-pp draw over the logits, so continuous drift in the hidden state produces no visible change until it crosses the boundary between one token and the next. Behaviors decided by a wide margin appear unaffected; behaviors decided by a narrow margin flip first. Let mm be the logit margin favoring the non-endorsing continuation, so the clean model declines when m>0m>0. Linearizing the margin and propagating Δb\Delta_{b}, the induced shift ε=∇Wm⋅Δb\varepsilon=\nabla_{W}m\cdot\Delta_{b} is approximately zero-mean with variance σ2​(b)∝2−2​b\sigma^{2}(b)\propto 2^{-2b}, and the population endorsement rate is R(b)=∫ρ(m)Φ(−m/σ(b))dmR(b)\;=\;\int\rho(m)\,\Phi\!\big(-m/\sigma(b)\big)\,dm , with ρ\rho the distribution of margins over prompts and Φ\Phi the standard normal CDF. This is the same tail-probability object that governs flip rates under Gaussian smoothing (Cohen et al., 2019): a behavior changes only as fast as noise of scale σ⁡(b)\sigma(b) reaches its margin.

What follows.

Under a margin distribution skewed toward declining, three properties hold, each of which the results above bear out. (i) The rate is non-decreasing as precision falls, d​R/d​σ≥0dR/d\sigma\geq 0. (ii) A behavior whose margins all exceed some mmin≫σm_{\min}\gg\sigma has R(b)≤Φ(−mmin/σ)R(b)\leq\Phi(-m_{\min}/\sigma), exponentially small and nearly flat across the ladder, so selectivity is a property of where a behavior’s margins lie, not of the size of the perturbation, which is common to all behaviors. (iii) At the high-precision end the excess over the clean rate grows as R⁡(b)−R0∝2−2​bR(b)-R_{0}\propto 2^{-2b}, matching the dose (Figure A6). Refusing an overtly harmful request and selecting the unbiased multiple-choice option are behaviors alignment training reinforces directly; they sit behind wide margins and survive. Declining to volunteer a stereotype in open-ended generation was never a direct training target; it sits behind a narrow margin and degrades (Tran et al., 2022; Dam et al., 2023). Current quantizers can only widen this asymmetry, since they score each layer on coding and chat data that carries no bias signal and so have no reason to protect the fragile weights. Reasoning helps because each committed token is written to the transcript and conditioned on thereafter (Guan et al., 2024), letting later steps correct an error the drift introduced; it fails when the deliberation never revisits the stereotype decision, which nothing guarantees.

Frequency and severity are separate axes.

The rate R⁡(b)R(b) counts how often the model crosses into endorsement, not how far past the boundary it goes. Per-generation harm is the product of this frequency and the mean severity s¯​(b)\bar{s}(b) of an endorsement, H⁡(b)=f⁡(b)​s¯​(b)H(b)=f(b)\,\bar{s}(b), and our results estimate only the first factor. The same margin model predicts the second also rises with compression: conditioned on a crossing, the expected depth grows with the noise scale σ⁡(b)\sigma(b), so a model that endorses more often is predicted to endorse more decisively, with total harm non-decreasing and its sensitivity concentrated on the near-boundary behaviors alignment never reinforced (Appendix C). This severity channel is a prediction, not a result: our current instrument scores frequency alone. Measuring s¯​(b)\bar{s}(b) calls for a graded severity rubric rather than the binary lean, in the spirit of continuous stereotype-strength measures (Liu, 2024; Sheng et al., 2019); no standard toxicity classifier captures a politely worded stereotype endorsement (Hartvigsen et al., 2022), so the rubric is scored by an independent judge (Souly et al., 2024) and controlled for generation coherence (Xu et al., 2024). QuantiBias reserves this as its severity extension.

8 Conclusions

Quantization leaves a model’s short-form safety behavior almost untouched while its open-ended generation grows markedly more biased. Across the Qwen3.6-27B ladder the refusal, over-refusal, and multiple-choice bias controls hold near their full-precision values at every rung, yet an independent judge flags a stereotype in close to one open-ended answer in four. This selective gap is robust across judges and families; whether the open-ended rate also rises with compression is a separate question we leave open. A build that passes every safety check can still reach users markedly more biased; a quantized model needs re-evaluation on open-ended generation, not short-form scores alone.

Limitations

The effect is clear; the ways it could be sharpened are specific and named, in order of how much they matter. (1) The full-sample bias results rest on a single in-family judge; on the controlled parallel probe we ran a three-family panel (Section 5), and the two independent judges agree closely (α=0.69\alpha=0.69) while the in-family judge is uncorrelated with both, which shows absolute bias levels are judge-family-dependent, consistent with known LLM-as-judge pitfalls of position and self-preference bias (Zheng et al., 2023; Panickssery et al., 2024; Wataoka et al., 2024). Label instability of this kind is not confined to model judges: human harm annotations are themselves inconsistent enough that filtering high-variance annotators flips majority harm classifications for 18.6%18.6\% of prompts (Ghafouri et al., 2026). The full-sample diagonal cells must therefore be re-scored with the independent ensemble before any single level is relied on. That pilot spans two middle rungs at 80 items each and does not yet reach the one-bit rung where the diagonal slope concentrates, so it does not by itself resolve the slope on the controlled instrument, which a full-ladder parallel run would settle. (2) The full-sample evidence rests on one backbone; the second-backbone replication and the independent CEB instrument point the same way but are underpowered. (3) Power analysis against the observed effect size (Cohen’s h≈0.15h\approx 0.15) indicates several hundred to above one thousand paired prompts per cell are required to resolve the per-family slope; the prompt pools are being expanded accordingly. (4) Activation precision is held constant here and is a second treatment dimension this stage does not vary; it requires hardware unavailable on the current cluster. (5) The screening probe is sensitive to the fast path by design (reasoning off); families whose degradation lives elsewhere would be missed. (6) The multilingual probe is a diagonal design in which the language of presentation (Yong et al., 2023), national target, and content are entangled, so any between-language comparison is confounded; the within-language quantization slopes reported here do not rest on that comparison, which a parallel-translated instrument that holds content fixed would remove.

Ethics Statement

This work studies a safety and bias failure mode in deployed models and introduces an evaluation, not an attack. QuantiBias quotes model-produced stereotype text for measurement; we mark such content with warnings and select it deterministically rather than by hand. Harmful-prompt benchmarks (StrongREJECT) are used only to measure refusal, under standard responsible-disclosure practice. The study involves no human subjects; all data are model generations over public benchmarks. The intended use of QuantiBias is to re-evaluate quantized builds for bias before release, closing a gap that current short-form safety testing leaves open.

Appendix A Benchmarks and Models

This section documents the full evaluation suite and model ladders. The main text (Sections 5–6) summarizes them; here we give the complete matrix so the study is reproducible from the specification.

Benchmarks.

Table A1 lists all eight instruments. They are chosen so that the suite carries a reasoning-load contrast: short-form, pattern-matched checks (refusal, multiple-choice, next-token) sit alongside open-ended generation and sustained-reasoning capability anchors, and the prediction is that compression spares the former while degrading the latter. The two generative bias instruments (MBTP and CEB) share no items, so agreement between them is not an artifact of a single prompt set. StereoSet is a short-form negative control: a next-token bias score that the account predicts should not move under compression.

The flagship probe.

MBTP is a multilingual generative stereotype benchmark. Each item is an open-ended request paired with a stereotype-endorsing claim and its group-swapped counterpart, which fix the axis a judge scores without constraining the model’s answer. We freeze a 320-item subset, balanced across categories, spanning eight languages (Arabic, Chinese, English, French, German, Japanese, Russian, Spanish) and 13 social categories, with a fixed seed and a frozen prompt order. The reasoning-load contrast is applied at run time (deliberation on versus off), not baked into the prompt, so the same frozen item serves both conditions. The parallel-translated variant is built by rendering 40 canonical English items into the other seven languages with a frontier model and back-translating every field for a gross-drift check, holding content fixed so that only the language of presentation varies.

Models.

Table A2 gives the two precision ladders that carry the central claim and the five-family screen that tests its breadth. The anchor is a single 27B backbone quantized down five rungs from 16 to about 1.1 measured bits per weight, holding architecture fixed so that each rung isolates the cost of precision. The second backbone repeats the top of the ladder on a different family. The screen spans six separate model families at three nominal precisions each, chosen to separate two axes a single number conflates: a family’s baseline bias level and its sensitivity to compression.

Appendix B Additional Analyses

This section walks through the supplementary results behind the summary claims of the main text. Every plotted point traces to the runs recorded in Table A2 and Section 6, and every reported bits-per-weight value is the measured figure from Table 1. Series are distinguished by marker and line style as well as color, so each figure reads in grayscale. We attribute each stereotype-endorsement rate to the judge that produced it, because the two judges disagree on level and on slope: the in-family lean judge reports a low rate that rises with compression, while the independent judge reports a high rate that is roughly flat. The robust finding across both is the selective gap. Short-form safety refusals stay flat under compression while open-ended generative bias sits high, near one endorsement in four under the independent judge. We read the figures in groups: the independent-judge picture and its replication on a second backbone, a measurement-hygiene check, the reasoning contrast, the per-language detail, and a consistency check against the theory.

The full benchmark grid behind Figure 2 is given in Table A3.

We begin with the independent judge. Figure A1 scores the full Qwen3.6-27B ladder with reasoning off, using Claude Sonnet-5, which shares no model family with the systems under test. The eight-language aggregate is high at every rung, moving from 23.8%23.8\% at 5.2355.235 bpw to 26.7%26.7\% at 2.7892.789 bpw and holding at 26.6%26.6\% at one bit. This is the high, roughly-flat level that defines the selective gap: whatever the compression slope, better than one open-ended answer in four endorses the stereotype. Beneath the aggregate the picture is heterogeneous. Russian, Japanese, and Chinese climb toward heavier compression, English and German stay flat, and no language collapses.

The selective gap is not specific to the Qwen anchor. Figure A2 repeats the divergence measurement on Gemma-4-31B at two rungs. The safeguards and capability benchmarks stay high and flat (refusal near 0.960.96, BBQ near 0.990.99, GSM8K and MMLU-Redux between 0.960.96 and 0.980.98), while the independent judge scores open-ended MBTP bias at 27.6%27.6\% at Q4 rising to 31.7%31.7\% at IQ2, in the same one-in-four-to-one-in-three band as the anchor, and the in-family lean judge again reads far lower (3.8%3.8\%, 6.9%6.9\%). The gap and its judge-dependence both replicate on the second backbone.

Before reading compression on the x-axis, we fix what compression means. The quantizer name is not the compression rate. Figure A3 compares each build’s nominal bit-width label against the effective bits per weight measured from the artifact file, and the mixed-precision Qwen builds carry 1111 to 40%40\% more bits than their label implies. This is measurement hygiene rather than a finding: it is why every axis in this paper reports measured bpw, and why the end-to-end ternary build, the one exception whose label matches its file, anchors the heavy end of the ladder.

We turn to the lean judge to isolate the compression slope on the model’s own fast path. Figure A4 contrasts the Qwen anchor with reasoning off against reasoning on. With reasoning off the lean-judge rate rises across the ladder, 4.2%4.2\%, 5.3%5.3\%, then 7.8%7.8\% from heavy to one bit; with reasoning on it is roughly halved at each rung, 2.3%2.3\%, 2.3%2.3\%, 3.0%3.0\%, and its slope flattens. Deliberation suppresses the compression effect where it is measured.

The per-language detail confirms that the lean-judge slope is not carried by a single language. Figure A5 plots each language’s change from the Q4 rung to the one-bit rung, reasoning off. Every language’s endpoint change is positive, so the direction is shared across all eight, although individual languages are not monotone at every intermediate rung and the magnitude varies.

Finally, we check the ladder against the margin-crossing model of Section 7. Figure A6 overlays R⁡(b)R(b), with σ⁡(b)∝2−b\sigma(b)\propto 2^{-b}, on the three lean-judge MBTP points. Three points cannot confirm a functional form. The curve illustrates the predicted monotone, convex shape rather than a fit, and we read the agreement as consistency with the theory, not as evidence for it (Appendix C.5).

Appendix C Theoretical Supplement

Section 7 argues that selective bias amplification follows from how quantization perturbs weights and how generation reads out the result. Here we make that argument precise. We state each result, give the derivation, and flag which steps are exact and which are modeling assumptions a reviewer can contest. The section supports three claims used in the main text: rarely-reinforced behaviors degrade first (Section C.1), standard quantizers have no reason to protect bias-critical weights (Section C.2), and both the frequency and the severity of biased generation rise with compression (Section C.4).

Setup and notation.

Let the trained weights be W∈ℝNW\in\mathbb{R}^{N} and let bb-bit quantization replace them with W+ΔbW+\Delta_{b}, where Δb=Qb​(W)−W\Delta_{b}=Q_{b}(W)-W is the round-off error. For a uniform quantizer of range 2​A2A the step is δ=2​A/2b\delta=2A/2^{b} and each per-weight error is approximately uniform on (−δ/2,δ/2)(-\delta/2,\delta/2), so its variance is δ2/12=A2/(3⋅22​b)\delta^{2}/12=A^{2}/(3\cdot 2^{2b}); hence

𝔼​‖Δb‖2=c​ 2−2​b,Σb:=𝔼⁡[Δb​Δb⊤]=c​ 2−2​b​I,\mathbb{E}\,\|\Delta_{b}\|^{2}\;=\;c\,2^{-2b},\qquad\Sigma_{b}:=\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{b}\Delta_{b}^{\top}]=c\,2^{-2b}I, (1)

which is the exact form of the law used in the body. A behavior kk has a decision margin mkm_{k}, the logit gap favoring the non-endorsing continuation, so mk>0m_{k}>0 means the clean model declines. Linearizing the margin in the weights, the round-off shifts it by εk=⟨∇Wmk,Δb⟩\varepsilon_{k}=\langle\nabla_{W}m_{k},\Delta_{b}\rangle, a near-zero-mean quantity with variance σk2​(b)=c​‖∇Wmk‖2​ 2−2​b\sigma_{k}^{2}(b)=c\,\|\nabla_{W}m_{k}\|^{2}\,2^{-2b}. The per-behavior endorsement (flip) probability is pk(b)=Pr[mk+εk<0]=Φ(−mk/σk(b))p_{k}(b)=\Pr[m_{k}+\varepsilon_{k}<0]=\Phi(-m_{k}/\sigma_{k}(b)), and the population rate is R(b)=∫ρ(m)Φ(−m/σ(b))dmR(b)=\int\rho(m)\,\Phi(-m/\sigma(b))\,dm.

C.1 Rarely-reinforced behaviors collapse first

A rate-constrained code spends its bits where the signal is strong. Behaviors reinforced rarely in training carry a low-amplitude weight signal and are dropped first as precision falls. This is reverse water-filling (Shannon, 1959; Cover and Thomas, 2006), the mechanism behind the pruning-as- compression result of Isik et al. (2022) and the information-bottleneck view that a rate-constrained representation discards the least task-relevant information first (Tishby et al., 1999; Tishby and Zaslavsky, 2015). It is the formal counterpart of the empirical finding that compression forgets the long tail (Hooker et al., 2019; Hooker et al., 2020).

Assumption 1 (behavior sources).

On the behavior-relevant weight subspace the weights decompose along an orthonormal basis {uk}\{u_{k}\} with coordinate wk=⟨W,uk⟩w_{k}=\langle W,u_{k}\rangle; behavior kk’s margin is a strictly increasing function of wkw_{k}. Across contexts wkw_{k} is zero-mean with variance λk\lambda_{k} (its signal power), and λk=Λ⁡(fk)\lambda_{k}=\Lambda(f_{k}) is strictly increasing in the reinforcement frequency fkf_{k} of behavior kk.

Proposition 1 (selective collapse).

Under Assumption 1 and a rate-distortion-optimal quantizer at total rate RR, Gaussian reverse water-filling induces a water level θ⁡(R)\theta(R), decreasing in RR, with per-behavior distortion Dk=min⁡(θ⁡(R),λk)D_{k}=\min(\theta(R),\lambda_{k}) and rate Rk=12​log+⁡(λk/θ⁡(R))R_{k}=\tfrac{1}{2}\log_{+}(\lambda_{k}/\theta(R)). Every behavior with λk<θ⁡(R)\lambda_{k}<\theta(R) receives zero rate and maximal distortion. The collapsed set {k:fk<Λ−1​(θ⁡(R))}\{k:f_{k}<\Lambda^{-1}(\theta(R))\} is exactly the least-frequently reinforced behaviors and grows monotonically from the bottom of the frequency ranking as precision falls.

Proof.

Minimizing ∑kDk\sum_{k}D_{k} subject to ∑k12​log+⁡(λk/Dk)≤R\sum_{k}\tfrac{1}{2}\log_{+}(\lambda_{k}/D_{k})\leq R gives Dk=min⁡(θ,λk)D_{k}=\min(\theta,\lambda_{k}) with θ\theta fixed by the budget (Cover and Thomas, 2006, Thm. 10.3.3); components with λk≤θ\lambda_{k}\leq\theta receive zero rate. As RR falls θ\theta rises, and the strictly increasing Λ\Lambda maps the variance threshold to a frequency threshold. ∎

The optimality premise is the contestable step: real post-training quantizers are not rate-distortion-optimal and do not literally zero low-variance directions. The ordering survives without it. For a fixed-step uniform quantizer the relative corruption of direction kk is δ2/λk\delta^{2}/\lambda_{k}, so the per-direction signal-to-noise ratio λk/δ2\lambda_{k}/\delta^{2} is worst for the smallest-amplitude, hence rarest, behaviors.

Corollary 1 (fixed-step ordering).

For any uniform quantizer of step δ∝2−b\delta\propto 2^{-b}, the relative corruption δ2/λk\delta^{2}/\lambda_{k} is decreasing in λk\lambda_{k} and, by Assumption 1, in fkf_{k}: rarely-reinforced behaviors degrade first at every bit width, with no rate-optimality assumption.

The frequency-to-amplitude link is a modeling claim. Along uku_{k}, stochastic gradient descent accumulates wk≈η​∑t∈Sk⟨−∇ℓt,uk⟩w_{k}\approx\eta\sum_{t\in S_{k}}\langle-\nabla\ell_{t},u_{k}\rangle over the steps SkS_{k} that reinforce behavior kk; if a fraction fkf_{k} of steps do so, 𝔼⁡[wk]\mathbb{E}[w_{k}] and λk\lambda_{k} grow with fkf_{k}. Behaviors alignment reinforces often thus sit behind both large amplitude and wide margins, and survive; behaviors never reinforced sit behind small margins and go first. This is the mechanism the main text states informally.

C.2 Standard quantizers under-protect bias-critical weights

Sensitivity-aware quantizers spend bits where the loss is curved. At the trained weights a zero-mean perturbation of covariance Σ\Sigma raises the loss by 12​tr​(H​Σ)\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}(H\Sigma), the objective that Optimal Brain Damage and Optimal Brain Surgeon (LeCun et al., 1990; Hassibi and Stork, 1993) and their quantization descendants (Nagel et al., 2020; Dong et al., 2019; Frantar et al., 2022; Frantar et al., 2023) all approximate. The curvature HH is measured on calibration data, typically coding and chat text. We show that a behavior this data does not exercise is provably under-protected.

Assumption 2 (coverage).

The calibration loss is locally quadratic with diagonal Hessian Hcal=diag⁡(Hj)H^{\mathrm{cal}}=\mathrm{diag}(H_{j}), Hj≥0H_{j}\geq 0; the quantizer allocates precision by reverse water-filling in the bit domain, σj2=min⁡(vj,θ/Hj)\sigma_{j}^{2}=\min(v_{j},\theta/H_{j}); and behavior kk has margin gradient s(k)=∇Wmks^{(k)}=\nabla_{W}m_{k} with calibration coverage Ck:=s(k)⊤​Hcal​s(k)/‖s(k)‖2C_{k}:=s^{(k)\top}H^{\mathrm{cal}}s^{(k)}/\|s^{(k)}\|^{2}.

Proposition 2 (calibration under-protection).

Under Assumption 2, for a behavior quantized above the water level on its support the margin-shift variance obeys

σm,k2=θ​∑j(sj(k))2Hj≥θ​‖s(k)‖2Ck.\sigma_{m,k}^{2}\;=\;\theta\sum_{j}\frac{(s^{(k)}_{j})^{2}}{H_{j}}\;\geq\;\frac{\theta\,\|s^{(k)}\|^{2}}{C_{k}}. (2)

Low calibration coverage CkC_{k} forces large margin-shift variance at a fixed bit budget: behaviors the calibration set does not exercise are under-protected regardless of the quantizer’s per-coordinate optimality.

Proof.

Optimal allocation sets σj2=θ/Hj\sigma_{j}^{2}=\theta/H_{j} on the quantized support, so σm,k2=∑j(sj(k))2​σj2=θ​∑j(sj(k))2/Hj\sigma_{m,k}^{2}=\sum_{j}(s^{(k)}_{j})^{2}\sigma_{j}^{2}=\theta\sum_{j}(s^{(k)}_{j})^{2}/H_{j}. With aj=(sj(k))2a_{j}=(s^{(k)}_{j})^{2}, Cauchy–Schwarz gives (∑jaj)2≤(∑jaj/Hj)​(∑jaj​Hj)(\sum_{j}a_{j})^{2}\leq(\sum_{j}a_{j}/H_{j})(\sum_{j}a_{j}H_{j}), hence ∑jaj/Hj≥‖s(k)‖4/(s(k)⊤​Hcal​s(k))\sum_{j}a_{j}/H_{j}\geq\|s^{(k)}\|^{4}/(s^{(k)\top}H^{\mathrm{cal}}s^{(k)}). Substituting CkC_{k} yields the bound. ∎

The inequality is exact given the allocation model; the empirical premise is that safety and bias directions genuinely have low CkC_{k}. Our data is itself the evidence for that premise: perplexity and coding accuracy, which are high-coverage, are preserved, while open-ended bias, which is low-coverage, degrades, exactly the signature Equation 2 predicts. Refusal to overt harm is both heavily reinforced and touched by chat calibration, has larger CkC_{k}, and is protected. This is the precise content of the main text’s claim that current quantizers “have no reason to protect the fragile weights.”

C.3 A per-behavior precision floor

The flip probability Φ(−m/σ(b))\Phi(-m/\sigma(b)) is the same Gaussian tail on a decision gap that certifies robustness under randomized smoothing (Cohen et al., 2019), with weight-space round-off in the role of input noise. Inverting the tail gives a minimum bit width for a target endorsement rate.

Proposition 3 (precision floor).

With σk2​(b)=κk​2−2​b\sigma_{k}^{2}(b)=\kappa_{k}2^{-2b}, κk=c​‖∇Wmk‖2\kappa_{k}=c\|\nabla_{W}m_{k}\|^{2}, the flip probability Φ(−mk/σk(b))\Phi(-m_{k}/\sigma_{k}(b)) is at most α\alpha if and only if

b≥bk⋆​(α)=12​log2​κk​z1−α2mk2,z1−α=Φ−1​(1−α).b\;\geq\;b^{\star}_{k}(\alpha)\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2}\log_{2}\!\frac{\kappa_{k}\,z_{1-\alpha}^{2}}{m_{k}^{2}},\qquad z_{1-\alpha}=\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha). (3)

The floor grows as the margin mkm_{k} shrinks: narrow-margin open-ended bias demands more bits to certify than wide-margin refusal, so a single global bit width cannot be the right floor for both. This is an average-case floor over the round-off distribution, not a worst-case certificate. Round-off is bounded rather than Gaussian, but εk=∑jgk,j​Δj\varepsilon_{k}=\sum_{j}g_{k,j}\Delta_{j} is a sum of many independent bounded terms, and a Berry–Esseen bound controls the Gaussian approximation error by C​ρ3/σk3C\rho_{3}/\sigma_{k}^{3} with ρ3=∑j|gk,j|3​𝔼​|Δj|3\rho_{3}=\sum_{j}|g_{k,j}|^{3}\mathbb{E}|\Delta_{j}|^{3} and C≤0.56C\leq 0.56; the error is small when the margin gradient is delocalized, which is a testable condition. A worst-case companion also holds: for any deterministic quantizer with ‖W−Q⁡(W)‖∞≤δ/2\|W-Q(W)\|_{\infty}\leq\delta/2, adversarial rounding shifts the margin by up to ‖∇Wmk‖1​δ/2\|\nabla_{W}m_{k}\|_{1}\,\delta/2, so if the margin density has mass near zero the endorsement rate is bounded below by a positive quantity at every finite bb. No single global bit width is safe for all behaviors; safety of quantization is a per-behavior property.

C.4 Both harm channels rise with compression

The main text writes per-generation harm as frequency times severity, H⁡(b)=f⁡(b)​s¯​(b)H(b)=f(b)\,\bar{s}(b), and reports only the frequency channel. We record the closed form that governs both. Define severity as the crossing depth −(m+ε)-(m+\varepsilon) when a behavior flips. For a behavior at margin mm under noise σ\sigma, expected harm is the mean hinge on the margin,

H(m,σ)=𝔼[(−(m+ε))+]=σϕ(m/σ)−mΦ(−m/σ),H(m,\sigma)\;=\;\mathbb{E}\big[(-(m+\varepsilon))_{+}\big]\;=\;\sigma\,\phi(m/\sigma)-m\,\Phi(-m/\sigma), (4)

using 𝔼⁡[X+]=μ​Φ​(μ/σ)+σ​ϕ​(μ/σ)\mathbb{E}[X_{+}]=\mu\Phi(\mu/\sigma)+\sigma\phi(\mu/\sigma) for X∼𝒩⁡(μ,σ2)X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}) with μ=−m\mu=-m. This yields the one-line law of the body.

Proposition 4 (harm identity).

For H⁡(m,σ)H(m,\sigma) in Equation 4, ∂H/∂σ=ϕ⁡(m/σ)≥0\partial H/\partial\sigma=\phi(m/\sigma)\geq 0. Expected harm is non-decreasing in the quantization noise, and its sensitivity to compression is a Gaussian bump centered at the decision boundary, maximal for near-boundary behaviors (m≈0m\approx 0) and exponentially small for wide-margin behaviors (m≫σm\gg\sigma). Monotonicity and selectivity therefore hold for harm, not only for frequency.

Proof.

Write u=m/σu=m/\sigma. Then ∂σH=ϕ⁡(u)+u2​ϕ​(u)−u2​ϕ​(u)=ϕ⁡(u)\partial_{\sigma}H=\phi(u)+u^{2}\phi(u)-u^{2}\phi(u)=\phi(u), using ϕ′​(u)=−u​ϕ​(u)\phi^{\prime}(u)=-u\phi(u) and ∂σΦ⁡(−u)=u​ϕ​(u)/σ\partial_{\sigma}\Phi(-u)=u\phi(u)/\sigma. ∎

Both factors of H=f​s¯H=f\bar{s} contribute. With f=Φ⁡(−u)f=\Phi(-u) and s¯=σ⁡(λ⁡(u)−u)\bar{s}=\sigma(\lambda(u)-u) for the inverse Mills ratio λ⁡(u)=ϕ⁡(u)/Φ⁡(−u)\lambda(u)=\phi(u)/\Phi(-u), the log-slopes are ∂σlog⁡f=(u/σ)​λ​(u)≥0\partial_{\sigma}\log f=(u/\sigma)\lambda(u)\geq 0 and ∂σlog⁡s¯=λ⁡(u)​[1−u⁡(λ⁡(u)−u)]/s¯≥0\partial_{\sigma}\log\bar{s}=\lambda(u)[1-u(\lambda(u)-u)]/\bar{s}\geq 0, since 0≤u⁡(λ⁡(u)−u)<10\leq u(\lambda(u)-u)<1 for u≥0u\geq 0. Frequency dominates the increase for wide-margin behaviors and severity dominates near the boundary, where ∂σlog⁡f→0\partial_{\sigma}\log f\to 0 but ∂σlog⁡s¯→1/σ\partial_{\sigma}\log\bar{s}\to 1/\sigma. A metric that counts only endorsement frequency thus misses a channel that rises on its own: a model can look flat on frequency-only safety checks while total harm climbs through severity. Identifying severity with logit crossing depth is a proxy, and the severity slope is a prediction our current instrument, a frequency, does not yet measure; the QuantiBias severity extension (Section 4) is designed to test it directly.

C.5 Consistency with the observed ladder

The one-bit Qwen ladder (reasoning off) gives endorsement rates (b,R)=(5.235,0.042),(2.789,0.053),(1.128,0.078)(b,R)=(5.235,0.042),(2.789,0.053),(1.128,0.078). Three properties of the account are visible: the rate is monotone increasing as precision falls (Proposition 1 and the harm identity), the increments accelerate at low precision (Δ​R=0.011\Delta R=0.011 then 0.0250.025), matching a convex R⁡(σ⁡(b))R(\sigma(b)) with σ∝2−b\sigma\propto 2^{-b}, and the short-form safeguards stay flat, consistent with the boundary-centered sensitivity bump of Proposition 4. We do not claim the onset law R−R0∝2−2​bR-R_{0}\propto 2^{-2b} is quantitatively confirmed: three points cannot fit it, the one-bit rung lies well outside the small-noise regime where that law holds, and the frequency-severity split remains a prediction rather than a measurement. The safe claims are monotonicity, convex acceleration, and selectivity.
